stops.name: The court of Solomon, Sheba and the Temple faced across the atlas
stops.campa: The myth the opera enters is Jerusalem in the age of the Temple: this stop faces our Sheba and Solomon journeys at once. The Queen of the South comes with camels bearing spices and gold to prove the wise king with hard questions; and behind them both stands the builder, Hiram-Adoniram, whose bronze pillars Jachin and Boaz frame the sanctuary door. Where scripture makes Sheba a marvel of homage and Hiram a craftsman of the first Temple, Barbier's libretto binds the three in a single tragic knot, queen, king, and artisan, and hands the Masonic Temple-legend to the operatic stage.
stops.quote: And when the queen of Sheba had seen all Solomon's wisdom... there was no more spirit in her.
stops.quote_source: 1 Kings 10, the scriptural source-world the libretto dramatizes

stops.name: Opéra-Comique (Salle Favart), MIGNON: Goethe again, the song of the South
stops.campa: On 17 November 1866 the Salle Favart gives Ambroise Thomas's Mignon, Barbier and Carré after Goethe's Wilhelm Meister: Goethe made song a second time. Célestine Galli-Marié is the waifish Mignon, the stolen Italian child who does not know her own country, and she sings the ache of it: 'Connais-tu le pays où fleurit l'oranger,' do you know the land where the orange flowers, the land of golden fruit and an eternal spring. It is Goethe's 'Kennst du das Land,' the very longing for the lemon-blossoming South that would one day drive Goethe himself across the Alps.
stops.quote: Connais-tu le pays où fleurit l'oranger, le pays des fruits d'or et des roses vermeilles... C'est là, c'est là que je voudrais vivre, aimer, aimer et mourir !
stops.quote_source: Mignon (Thomas), Act I, libretto Barbier & Carré, after Goethe

stops.name: Italy of the lemon-flower, Mignon's country, faced toward Goethe's Italian Journey
stops.campa: The country Mignon cannot name is Italy, and this stop faces Goethe's own Italian Journey. The land where the orange flowers, where the marble men beckon in the golden hall, where light boats glide like birds on a transparent lake, Goethe put that longing in his novel, and then obeyed it, slipping over the Brenner in 1786 toward Verona, Venice, Rome. Barbier's French carries the same yearning across another frontier and another art. Two journeys meet here: Goethe's real one south to the sun, and Mignon's sung one, homeward to a country she was stolen from and can only remember in song.
stops.quote: Kennst du das Land, wo die Zitronen blühn, im dunkeln Laub die Gold-Orangen glühn?
stops.quote_source: Goethe, Wilhelm Meisters Lehrjahre III, the German source Barbier translated

stops.name: Théâtre-Lyrique (Place du Châtelet), ROMÉO ET JULIETTE
stops.campa: On 27 April 1867, in the new Théâtre-Lyrique on the Place du Châtelet, Gounod's Roméo et Juliette opens to the words of Barbier and Carré, as the Universal Exposition fills Paris with the world. Miolan-Carvalho is Juliette; the opera is a garland of duets, the lovers meeting and parting and meeting in song: 'Nuit d'hyménée, ô douce nuit d'amour!' Shakespeare's Verona is remade for the French pit, the balcony and the tomb strung between four love-duets. It is among Gounod's greatest triumphs, and the pair's Shakespeare turned wholly to music.
stops.quote: Nuit d'hyménée ! Ô douce nuit d'amour ! La destinée m'enchaîne à toi sans retour.
stops.quote_source: Roméo et Juliette (Gounod), Act IV duet, libretto Barbier & Carré, after Shakespeare

stops.name: Opéra (Salle Le Peletier), HAMLET: the ghost and Ophelia's drowning
stops.campa: On 9 March 1868 the Salle Le Peletier gives Ambroise Thomas's Hamlet, Barbier and Carré after Shakespeare: the last great creation on that stage before it burned and the Garnier rose. Jean-Baptiste Faure is the brooding prince; Christine Nilsson is Ophélie, whose mad scene is the opera's glory: she wanders to the water's edge, sings her broken song to the willows, and drowns among the flowers. The ghost on the ramparts, the play within the play, the poisoned court: Shakespeare's darkest tragedy given a French tongue and, at the last, a French crown.
stops.quote: Partagez-vous mes fleurs !... À vous cette humble branche de romarin sauvage.
stops.quote_source: Hamlet (Thomas), Act IV, Ophélie's mad scene, libretto Barbier & Carré

stops.name: Elsinore of the mad Ophelia, the drowning faced as myth
stops.campa: The myth the opera enters stands on the cold battlements of Elsinore, where the murdered king walks and the prince feigns madness to unmask him. But the image that Barbier's verse fixes forever is Ophelia at the brook: her wits undone by grief and betrayal, she garlands herself with crow-flowers and long purples, climbs the leaning willow, and slips singing into the weedy water: 'her clothes spread wide, and mermaid-like awhile they bore her up.' Shakespeare's report becomes, in the opera, a scene we witness: madness set to a French coloratura, death by water made visible song.
stops.quote: There is a willow grows aslant a brook... There on the pendent boughs her coronet weeds clambering to hang, an envious sliver broke.
stops.quote_source: Shakespeare, Hamlet IV.vii, the source Barbier dramatized as Ophélie's mad scene

stops.name: Paris besieged, the theatres dark, the Franco-Prussian War
stops.campa: On 19 September 1870 the Prussian armies close the ring around Paris, and the lyric city falls silent. Sedan has fallen, the Empire is gone, the Republic proclaimed; through the long winter the capital starves, the theatres go dark, and the librettist's trade stops with them. There are no premieres now, only cold and cannon. The world that Carré and Barbier had filled with Faust and Juliette and Ophélie is a besieged city eating its zoo animals. It is an interruption in the poet's whole life: the one stretch of years when the myths cannot be made song.

stops.name: The Commune and the burning, the Théâtre-Lyrique in flames
stops.campa: In the last days of May 1871 the Commune goes down in fire. As the government troops fight into the city, the Théâtre-Lyrique on the Place du Châtelet, where only four years before Roméo had sung to Juliette, burns to its walls on 25 May. The Tuileries, the Hôtel de Ville, whole quarters go up; Paris versifies its own tragedy in smoke. The stage that had carried Barbier's Shakespeare into song is a ruin. From this ash, the Third Republic will rise, and will look for something to console it. The librettist has an answer waiting: a maid of Lorraine.

stops.name: Argenteuil, the death of Michel Carré, the two-headed pen halved
stops.campa: On 28 June 1872, at Argenteuil on the Seine below Paris, Michel Carré dies. For more than twenty years the two names had been one signature, Carré et Barbier, so fused that no one could part their lines; now the pen is halved. Barbier will write on alone for thirty years more, and give some of his greatest work solo: the Contes d'Hoffmann, the Jeanne d'Arc. But the great collaborative engine of the Second Empire lyric stage is stopped. The survivor carries both names forward the way a widower carries a wedding ring: the myths still made song, but by one hand now.

stops.name: Théâtre de la Gaîté, JEANNE D'ARC: Joan as France's consolation
stops.campa: On 8 November 1873, at the Théâtre de la Gaîté by the square des Arts-et-Métiers, Barbier's own five-act verse drama Jeanne d'Arc is given with music by Gounod: this is Barbier not adapting but writing, his own alexandrines for the Maid. After the humiliation of 1870 and the amputation of Alsace-Lorraine, Joan of Lorraine returns to the Paris stage as the nation's wounded conscience: the peasant girl who heard the voices, drove out the invader, and burned for France. This stop faces our Joan of Arc journey directly: the martyr of Rouen made, in a beaten Paris, a promise of resurrection.
stops.quote: Filles de Lorraine, la Vierge est là qui vous appelle... pour la France, priez !
stops.quote_source: Jeanne d'Arc (Gounod), drame en cinq actes et en vers de Jules Barbier, 1873

stops.name: Domrémy and Rouen, the Maid's myth faced across the atlas
stops.campa: The myth the drama enters begins in a village of Lorraine and ends in the market-square of Rouen. This stop faces our Joan of Arc journey: the girl of Domrémy who at thirteen hears Saint Michael and Saint Catherine in her father's garden, cuts her hair, takes the sword, lifts the siege of Orléans, and crowns her king at Reims, then is sold, tried, and burned at nineteen, her ashes cast into the Seine. Barbier gives France, humbled in 1870, her holiest patriot back: not as history but as consolation, the martyr who proves the nation can rise from its own fire.
stops.quote: Voices? — I heard them well. They came from God.
stops.quote_source: Joan of Arc, trial of condemnation, 1431, the source-figure Barbier dramatized

stops.name: Opéra (Palais Garnier), POLYEUCTE: the Christian martyr
stops.campa: On 7 October 1878, in the year-old Palais Garnier, Gounod's Polyeucte is given to Barbier and Carré's verse after Corneille: the work Gounod loved above all his own, dreamed of years before in a church on the Via Appia. Polyeucte, newly baptized, smashes the pagan idols and will not recant though his wife Pauline pleads and the tribunal threatens; he goes to his death singing his faith. Corneille's great Christian tragedy is remade for the Opéra. But the age has cooled; the martyr fails to move the pit, and the work closes after twenty-nine nights: 'the sorrow of my life,' Gounod said.
stops.quote: Source délicieuse, en misères féconde, que vous versez de maux sur ceux qui vous font Dieu !
stops.quote_source: Polyeucte (Gounod), after Corneille, the stances Barbier adapted for the martyr
